subtype: Approach: dreaming up ideas and then choosing one [Thinking]
passage: Indu's birthday was two weeks away, and she had three ideas written in her notebook in their small Mumbai flat: a movie on the laptop, a treasure hunt, a pizza party. Her friend Nazia sat on the bed, swinging her legs. "Okay," Indu said, tapping her pen. "Pizza for ten costs a lot. Papa will make a face. The movie is cheap, but everyone just sits, and ten people won't fit on our floor facing one laptop." She drew a line through both. "Treasure hunt. Clues can go in the kitchen, under the mattress, behind the curtain, even on the landing. It doesn't need a big room, and everyone runs around." Nazia grinned. "Can I hide the clues?"

qa.q: Where could the treasure hunt clues go?
qa.a: In the kitchen, under the mattress, behind the curtain, even on the landing.

qa.q: How was Indu feeling as she crossed out the pizza and the movie?
qa.a: She seemed thoughtful and decisive, then pleased once she saw the treasure hunt fit their small flat.

qa.q: What else could Indu weigh before settling on the treasure hunt?
qa.a: How long it takes and whether neighbours mind clues on the landing; comparing cost, space and fun is what made her choice sensible.

qa.q: How does Nazia see Indu's choice?
qa.a: Nazia grins and wants to hide the clues, so Nazia is clearly excited about the treasure hunt.

"Vijay, help me choose. Party ideas: treasure hunt, movie, pizza."
"Pizza! Obviously."
"Pizza for twelve? Mummy said we have to keep it simple."
"Okay... movie?"
"Twelve kids on our sofa? It seats three."
"So they sit on the floor."
"Our floor is the size of a carpet, Vijay." Trisha counted on her fingers. "Cost: treasure hunt is cheapest, just paper and a small prize. Space: clues can go anywhere, even the bathroom. Fun: everyone runs around."

"Can I write the clues?"

Papa agreed to order the cake from the bakery near the market. His elder brother Vijay, groaning, took decorations. "And games?" Pradeep asked. "Dadi," said Mummy. "She knows fifty." That left invitations. Pradeep smiled. He was the best drawer in 5B. He spent Sunday afternoon making twelve cards, each with a different cartoon animal holding a balloon, and ticked 'invitations' off the list himself.

subtype: Approach: planning only the fun parts and ignoring food and time [Pitfall]
passage: For next year, written after Lalremsiami's party, Saturday. She planned five games herself, and they were good ones: sack race, treasure hunt, dumb charades, a quiz, musical chairs. But the plan had no snacks and no times. By 5 pm the children were hungry and cranky; Abhinav was lying on the floor saying he was starving. I sent out for samosas, but the treasure hunt was still going at 6:30 when parents started ringing the bell. Two families left before the cake was cut. Lalremsiami cried in her room afterwards. Next year I'll sit with her and we'll put times and food on the list first.

qa.q: What time did parents start ringing the bell?
qa.a: At 6:30, while the treasure hunt was still going.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel after the party?
qa.a: She cried in her room, so she felt hurt and disappointed that families left before the cake and the day went wrong.

qa.q: What would you add first to Lalremsiami's plan next year?
qa.a: A snack time and a rough length for each game, so guests are fed and the cake happens before pickup.

qa.q: What was the party like for Abhinav?
qa.a: Abhinav was so hungry by 5 pm that he lay on the floor saying he was starving, so the games stopped being fun for him.

grounding: Shows a girl who planned five games but no snacks or timings, so guests got hungry at 5 pm and games ran past pickup time.

subtype: Approach: planning only the fun parts and ignoring food and time [Pitfall]
passage:
Sunday night
My party was today and I'm not happy. I planned everything fun: five games, prizes, a dance at the end. I didn't plan food except the cake, and I didn't think about how long anything would take. At five, Deepak asked, 'Is there anything to eat?' and then everyone was asking. Ammi ran to make pakoras, and the kitchen filled with smoke. The treasure hunt took an hour instead of twenty minutes, so we never did the dance. Then the parents came and waited in the doorway while we were still finding clues. Ammi said, 'Afreen beti, next time, snacks and a clock.' She's right.

qa.q: How long did the treasure hunt take?
qa.a: An hour instead of twenty minutes.

qa.q: How does Afreen feel about the day?
qa.a: Afreen feels unhappy and disappointed, because the fun she planned was spoiled by hunger and running out of time.

qa.q: What could Afreen try when planning her next party?
qa.a: Write a time next to each game and put snacks at a set point, like 'five o'clock: pakoras'; planning only the fun parts left gaps.

qa.q: How might the party have felt for the parents waiting in the doorway?
qa.a: They came at pickup time and had to stand waiting while clues were still being found, which may have been awkward and tiring.

grounding: Illustrates a girl planning only the games of her party, forgetting food and timings, so guests grow hungry and games overrun pickup.

subtype: Approach: preparing a plan B in case it rains [Thinking]
passage: Abhinav wanted his party at the mango orchard behind the village school, with races between the trees. He had drawn a map. Then his friend Afreen from next door, reading it, looked up at the sky. "It's the monsoon," she said. Abhinav frowned and thought out loud. "If it rains, the orchard turns to mud. Nobody will race. Then everyone goes home, and no party." He chewed his pencil. "Our front room. If we push the charpai and the trunk to the wall, there's space for musical chairs and dumb charades." He wrote 'PLAN B: front room' at the bottom of the map. On Saturday at four, the sky opened. By quarter past, twelve kids were shrieking round the chairs in the front room.

qa.q: Where did Abhinav want to hold his party?
qa.a: At the mango orchard behind the village school.

qa.q: What was Abhinav thinking when he chewed his pencil?
qa.a: He was worried rain would turn the orchard to mud and end the party, and was working out where else they could play.

qa.q: What else could Abhinav add to plan B?
qa.a: A few indoor games ready and a helper to move the charpai quickly; asking 'what if it rains?' early is what saved the party.

qa.q: How might Afreen see her remark about the monsoon?
qa.a: Afreen only mentioned the sky, but it led to plan B, so Afreen might feel pleased the comment helped save the party.

grounding: Shows a boy planning an outdoor party, asking what happens if it rains, and preparing the front room for indoor games so it isn't cancelled.

subtype: Approach: preparing a plan B in case it rains [Thinking]
passage: Paulo had planned everything for the park near his flat in Porto: football, a water-balloon fight, cake on the picnic table. The night before, lying in bed, a thought poked him. What if it rains? It rains a lot in Porto. If it rained, the park was useless, and his mother might just say, "Let's do it another weekend." He didn't want another weekend. He got up and found his sister Noa. "If it rains, can we clear the living room? Sofa against the wall, rug rolled up. Musical statues and a paper-plane contest." Noa shrugged. "I'll help push the sofa." Saturday dawned grey and wet. Paulo was already rolling up the rug.

qa.a: Football, a water-balloon fight and cake on the picnic table.

qa.q: Why did Paulo get up in the night?
qa.a: He felt worried that rain would get the party put off, and he didn't want to wait another weekend.

qa.q: What else could Paulo prepare for plan B?
qa.a: Paper for the planes and music for the statues game the night before; thinking 'what if it rains?' in advance is what kept the party on.

qa.q: How might Paulo's mother see plan B on the wet Saturday?
qa.a: She won't need to postpone, since the living room is ready, which may leave her relieved and impressed.

grounding: Illustrates a boy imagining rain spoiling his park party and planning to clear the living room for indoor games so it still happens.

subtype: Approach: imagining the party hour by hour in his head [Thinking]
passage:
Wednesday night
Party on Saturday! Tonight I lay in bed and played it like a film in my head. Guests arrive at 4. Balloons. Then a relay race in the courtyard. Then cake, then pass the parcel, then home at 6:30. It looked perfect... until I pictured my cousin Jyoti. She's so shy she hid behind Masi all through my last party. In a relay she'd just stand there. So I added one game: a team puppet show, with jobs: one to hold the curtain, one to move the puppets, one to do the sounds, one to clap the signals. Jyoti can do the sounds from behind the curtain. Nobody has to look at her. Masi always says, 'Vasudha, look after Jyoti.' I think she'll like this.

subtype: Approach: checking the budget with a parent and trimming [Revision]
passage: Disha, you want everything for your party, na? Let your Jyoti Bua tell you about my tenth birthday. I made a big list: balloons, a cream cake, and return gifts, those shiny boxes with toys inside. I took it to my Papa, and he sat down with me and added it all up. Then he showed me the envelope he'd kept for the party. The list came to more than the envelope. I sulked for one whole evening. The next day I sat with the list again. The shiny boxes went; instead, small pencil sets, two pencils and an eraser each. The balloons stayed, but the paper chains and stars I cut myself from coloured paper. My friends still talk about those stars.

subtype: Approach: insisting on copying a friend's grand party [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Pankaj came home from his classmate's party glowing. "A magician AND a bouncy castle! I want the same." His mother, Irawati, went quiet and said they'd talk.
Wednesday. They talked. The castle and the magician cost more than the family could manage. Pankaj slammed his door. "Then I don't want any party." He didn't come out for dinner.
Saturday. Up on the roof with his kite, Pankaj forgot to sulk long enough to notice he was happy. He thought: what do I actually like? Kites. Friends. Samosas. He ran downstairs. "Amma, can my party be a kite party on the roof?"

qa.a: Irawati went quiet on Monday and faced a slammed door on Wednesday, so she likely felt sad, then relieved when he asked for a kite party.

subtype: Approach: insisting on copying a friend's grand party [Pitfall]
passage: Tanvir, you're sulking because your friend had a magician? Sit. Your Thomas Uncle once did exactly the same. I was nine, in Kochi, and a classmate had a party with a magician who pulled a pigeon out of a hat, and a bouncy castle too. I went home and demanded both. My father, a bus conductor then, looked at the floor and said we couldn't. I cried, I refused my dinner, I said I'd have no party at all. Then my grandmother asked me, 'What do you like doing? You, not your classmate.' I said, 'Fishing in the backwaters, and football.' So my party was fishing off the jetty with four friends, and fried fish after. I still remember every fish.

qa.q: What did the magician pull out of a hat?
qa.a: A pigeon.

qa.q: How did young Thomas feel when his father said they couldn't?
qa.a: Young Thomas was upset and disappointed; he cried, refused dinner and said he'd have no party at all.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned things around?
qa.a: Answering his grandmother's question about what he himself liked, which led to a fishing party he still remembers.

qa.q: How might Thomas's father have felt saying no?
qa.a: He looked at the floor, so he probably felt sad and a little ashamed that he couldn't give his son what the classmate had.

grounding: Illustrates a boy demanding a classmate's grand party, being upset when the family cannot afford it, and finding joy in what he himself enjoys.

subtype: Approach: changing the game when guests look bored [Revision]
passage: Jahnavi, don't worry if a game flops at your party. Let your Grandma Lalremsiami tell you about my eleventh birthday in Aizawl. I had planned a quiet game: everyone sits in a circle of chairs and passes a whisper along. By the second round my friends were yawning, one was picking at her chair, two boys were poking each other. I saw it, and my stomach sank. So I stood up and said, 'Everyone outside! Catch-the-hen!' We ran round the garden, between the orange trees, shrieking, until my mother called us in for cake. Nobody remembered the whisper game. Everybody remembered the running.

qa.q: Where did they run during the new game?
qa.a: Round the garden, between the orange trees.

qa.q: How did young Lalremsiami feel when she saw her friends yawning?
qa.a: Her stomach sank, so she felt worried and disappointed that her quiet game was falling flat.

qa.q: What choice in the story saved the party?

qa.q: How did the friends seem to feel once they were outside?
qa.a: They were shrieking and running until cake, so they seemed happy and lively again.

grounding: Shows a birthday girl noticing restless friends during a quiet chair game and switching to a running game in the garden.

subtype: Approach: changing the game when guests look bored [Revision]

subtype: Approach: calming down before deciding what to do [Thinking]
passage: Last month my friend Madhav borrowed my new gel pen and gave it back with the tip squashed. He just laughed and said, 'It was already like that.' My face went so hot I could feel my ears. I had a whole speech ready, a mean one. But I knew if I opened my mouth then, I'd say something I couldn't take back. So I said nothing. At lunch I sat under the neem tree with my storybook instead of at our usual table. By the end of lunch my ears had cooled. I thought: Madhav probably pressed too hard, and maybe he was embarrassed. After school I said, 'Madhav, my pen broke. Can you be more careful?' He said sorry. Mummy said later, 'Simran beti, that was wise.'

qa.q: What did Madhav say about the pen?
qa.a: He laughed and said, 'It was already like that.'

qa.q: How did Simran feel when Madhav returned the squashed pen?
qa.a: Simran was so angry her face went hot and she could feel her ears, with a mean speech ready.

qa.q: What else could Simran do if she were still angry after lunch?
qa.a: Wait longer, or talk it over with a teacher or parent first; staying quiet while hot and speaking once calm is what kept the friendship.

qa.q: How might Madhav have experienced Simran's silence at lunch?
qa.a: Madhav may have noticed Simran sitting apart and felt uneasy, which could be why he said sorry after school.

grounding: Shows a girl who, hot with anger over a borrowed pen, stays silent, reads alone at lunch, and decides what to say once she is calm.

"No idea. He just walked off at lunch."

qa.q: How did the moment in the line feel for Manav?
qa.a: With everyone looking and rajma on his shirt, Manav probably felt embarrassed and hurt, and Siddharth's laugh felt like mockery.

subtype: Approach: working out what actually happened [Thinking]
passage: Last week Anand stopped sitting with me on the bus, and at first I was angry at him. What did I do? That night I lay awake and replayed the whole day like a video. Morning: fine. Maths: fine. Lunch: Anand tripped on the step and his tiffin burst open, idlis rolling across the floor. And I laughed. I remember now, I laughed loudly, because one idli rolled right into the Principal's office. But Anand didn't see that idli. He only saw his lunch on the floor and me laughing. No wonder. The next morning I didn't ask why he was sulking. I said, 'I wasn't laughing at you, but I shouldn't have laughed. Sorry.' He looked at me a long time, then said, 'Okay, Siddharth bhai. Sit.'
